narrative:
The model estimates a 55% chance that you will leave your job, which is why your promotion request has been denied. This probability is just over the tipping point, meaning the system sees enough warning signs to predict turnover rather than long-term retention.

Three factors stood out most in the decision. First, the number of training programs you attended in the last three years pushed the prediction most strongly toward staying. You completed seven or more, far above the typical employee the model expects to remain. Second, your overall career experience of 6–10 years pulled the prediction toward leaving. While this is common, it is less typical among people the model believes will stay, who are more often in the 1–5 year range. Third, the length of time you have spent in your current role also worked against the prediction, again because 6–10 years here is less common among those flagged as likely to stay.

Taken together, the model sees your solid training record as a reason you might stay, but views your experience level and tenure at the company as signals that you could be ready to move on. The organization should discuss your career goals openly with you and explore whether additional responsibilities, better recognition, or improved work-life support could increase your sense of belonging. You may also want to reflect on whether your current path still matches what you want long-term.
